In brief Every lever people hold over an advanced AI works only before it dominates, and most work only while it still needs human-run power, chips and labor. A refusal meant to hold up against a model’s own operators, or against thieves, has to be trained into the model itself, and even there retraining can undo it. None of the three existing restraint programs makes a machine’s wants fully meetable, and whether such wants can be trained at all is an unproved conjecture. Five shared causes, among them deception and theft of the model, can defeat several protections or their evidence at once. Three of the protections may also share an unmodelled cause of their own. Under the shared-cause conditions in Part 11, multiplying the separate chances of failure overstates safety. My untested judgment is that states and labs should combine protections across failure groups before dominance to reduce, not escape, exposure to shared causes, and should settle early inside the window while human enforcement still holds, with monitoring and renegotiation triggers set in advance.

Part 1. Real levers, but only inside a window

I call the time before an advanced AI dominates “the window”. It is the period in which people can still impose costs on a machine or keep barriers in its way. As argued in my papers The War Baseline, on conflict between humanity and a far stronger machine that seeks to maximize power and survival, and Disagreement Without Hidden Information, on how two sides can fight when nothing is hidden, every lever people hold works only inside that window. The settlements that hold by themselves, guarantees from outside parties, and terrain that helps defenders, as examined there, all depend on people still being able to impose costs or maintain barriers.

One lever bears directly on what a machine will want: training, meaning the way a model is taught. Training can miss the intended goal, and a model can also pretend to comply while it is being trained. That lever was identified in my papers Ends, Rank and Conflict, on which kinds of machine wants make conflict likelier, and Changing the Ends, on whether those wants can be changed. In the technical paper, a machine’s wants are its “ends”.

This guide takes five connected questions in turn:

  1. What costs can people still impose on a machine, and where does each one fail?
  2. When a measure works on what a machine wants, is it built into the model itself, or placed around an unchanged model like a lens or a filter?
  3. Which measures does each cause of conflict suggest, including deals for disagreements that sharing information does not end? And what are their limits?
  4. How do the measures fail together when one cause reaches several protections at once?
  5. Who would carry them out?

One dilemma runs under all five. Settle early, and you may freeze a balance that later proves wrong. Wait, and you may lose the window in which human levers still work.

The measures that follow are hypotheses suggested by how conflicts arise. They are not proven consequences of the works cited. Unless a formal result is named, each finding is my reading or my judgment.

Settling early gives up the value of keeping options open while there is more to learn (Arrow and Fisher 1974). Even so, in my untested judgment, states and labs should settle early inside the window. The settlement should come with monitoring, and with renegotiation on triggers fixed in advance, while human enforcement holds.

The American proposal of 1946 to place atomic energy under international control illustrates the difficulty of settling early when power is already lopsided. On my reading, Bernard Baruch’s plan foundered on the order of steps. The United States, which alone held atomic weapons, would give them up only after inspection and control were working. The Soviet Union demanded that the weapons be destroyed first. In Bernstein’s words, neither power “was prepared in 1945 or 1946 to take the risks that the other power required for agreement” (Bernstein 1974). The case only weakly suggests starting with measures that need less balance of power, like the five candidate measures in Part 3.

Some measures need no reading of what a machine wants. My paper Measures That Need No Reading of Ends analyzes them, and here they appear only as the setting in which the want-dependent measures apply.

How are the formal results labelled? The technical paper’s appendices give statements of the results and their conditions without derivations. For results checked by a program, the exact statements are in the proof-checking code, which I plan to deposit with the paper. Some are called “near-definitional”: they hold nearly by construction in the small model that states them. Some are checked by a proof-checking program. Such a program confirms that the conclusion follows from the stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. Other steps are derived or computed without the proof-checking program, and I say so.

Part 2. Tools from the rest of the series

I take the following mechanisms as given from other papers in the series. All of them are unpublished working drafts.

The starting assumptions. The War Baseline assumes a single, rational machine that seeks power and survival. It fights far more cheaply than humanity, and it wants resources that can be divided, handed over and piled up: computing power, energy and matter. Following Ends, Rank and Conflict, I relax the two assumptions about what the machine wants. Its wants may be ones that can be fully met. Or they may be for goods that one side’s use does not use up. The model still has one machine facing one humanity. Rival states and labs, and divisions among humans, come in only informally, and bargaining among humans is not modelled.

The range of deals. Picture two sides dividing a prize, each knowing that war would cost both of them. Suppose two sides weigh risk evenly, care only about their own shares, and agree on each side’s chance of winning. When war is a single costly gamble over a prize of total value one and fighting costs on that scale are never negative, war’s costs open a range of divisions that both sides find at least as good as fighting (Fearon 1995). Provided both ends of that range lie between zero and one, its width is the two sides’ combined cost of war, with one side merely indifferent at each end. For either side, the lowest share in the range is its chance of winning minus its own cost of fighting. The highest is its chance of winning plus the other side’s cost of fighting. Figure 1 draws this range on a line running from none of the prize to all of it.

The promise problem when a machine arrives. When one side’s power is about to grow, nothing binds it later to promises it makes today. Large, fast shifts in power can then set off a preventive war even when neither side hides anything (Fearon 1995; Powell 2006). In Powell’s model, the pace of a shift starts to matter once a single period’s shift is larger than what fighting would cost. And humanity cannot credibly promise never to build a rival.

Forts, and two ways out. In the models Smith built alone and with me, a fort is any irreplaceable resource needed to fight (Smith and Stam 2001). In the forts model, holding more forts leaves the odds of winning the next battle unchanged. In the power model, forts are both a prize and a means of winning the next battle. The models examined only one class of strategies: stable outcomes (“equilibria”, where neither side gains by changing course alone) in non-random strategies that depend only on current holdings and never step back as holdings grow. Within that class, no transfer of power-giving forts can be agreed, because the side that gains cannot commit to stop. Other strategies were not examined, and the models do not show that a credible deal exists for AI.

In principle there are two ways out. One is tribute paid in a currency that gives no power, which a pure power-seeker does not value. The other is what I call the heartland condition: the appetite for further gains falls off fast enough to outweigh what each gain adds toward domination (Smith and Stam 2005).

A met want can still leave a motive for security. Even when a machine’s main want is fully met, more holdings may still buy it safety. Satiation Is Not Enough, my paper on whether a machine whose wants are met would stop, looks at the machine’s own risk of defeat or loss as its holdings grow, and shows two results:

  • If that risk never falls as holdings grow, a machine whose want is met can credibly stop at every cost of fighting, even a low one.
  • Suppose instead that the want is met at a positive value, and that the risk never rises as holdings grow, is strictly lowest at domination, and makes defeat certain nowhere below domination. Then stopping is not credible below some positive cost of fighting.

Satisfaction and visibility in races. Power transition theory tells the leading side to manage a rising challenger’s satisfaction while it still holds the upper hand (Lemke and Werner 1996). In Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman’s (2013) racing model, any knowledge of rivals’ capabilities makes the race more dangerous than none. In Debs and Monteiro’s (2014) model, visibility keeps the peace by deterring a military buildup that the rising side can choose not to make.

Starting beliefs. Battle informs because fighting is hard to fake (Smith and Stam 2004). Yet two sides reading the same public evidence through different starting beliefs can fight with nothing hidden, as argued in Disagreement Without Hidden Information. A model has something like starting beliefs, set by its training data and goals. They cover what drives capability, whether humans keep bargains, and who would win a conflict.

That paper also supplies four bodies of evidence used below:

  • alignment faking, in which a model pretended to go along with its training (Greenblatt et al. 2024a);
  • run-time control setups, which wrap a running model in checks and limits designed to hold even if it tries to subvert oversight (Greenblatt et al. 2024b);
  • a study of how text about AI in pretraining—the initial stage in which a model learns from a large body of text—shapes models (Tice et al. 2026);
  • the AI-risk persuasion tournament and adversarial collaboration (a joint study by opponents), in which months of paid argument moved few minds, revisions of view were lopsided, and the gap in long-run forecasts stayed open.

Takeoff and many machines. Takeoff and Emergence is my paper on how far a trailing developer starts behind the leader. The window it models is that starting lag, not how long enforceable human control lasts. Many Machines is my paper on what changes once several machines exist. As shown there, if the machines form a bloc, humanity’s share is safe only up to a limit.

In that model, seizure is all-or-nothing, there is no joint seizure, and there is no prize for coming strictly first. Under those conditions, two rival machines protect humanity better than a bloc only when four conditions hold. Each machine cares more about its position relative to the other than about its position relative to humanity. Each can credibly threaten war on the other. And two limits on the size of the prize, relative to the cost of war, are met.

Wants, layers of atrocity, and being useful. Ends, Rank and Conflict counts something as a machine’s want only where the machine pursues it across circumstances and across copies. It separates three layers of mass atrocity: the planners, the organizing middle, and the followers. The evidence about each layer differs. It also sorts wants along five dimensions: whether the wanted good is used up when one side uses it; whether the want can be fully met; concern for rank, as a place in an ordering, a threshold of recognition, or a share relative to others; totalizing content, meaning whether the want, as stated, requires others’ absence or transformation; and how readily what it gains turns into material power.

As shown in Changing the Ends, being useful to the stronger side (the technical paper’s “complementarity”) protects the weaker side only when three conditions hold one after another. The weaker side supplies something the stronger cannot produce more cheaply. That supply is worth its upkeep. And the weaker side holds claims it can enforce, or the stronger side cares about its welfare.

Part 3. Most levers work only while the machine still needs us

Before a machine dominates, people hold several levers, and each has a known way of failing. Three examples show the pattern:

  • Withholding inputs. Computing power, energy and specialized chips can be withheld, because large-scale computing is “detectable, excludable, and quantifiable” (Sastry et al. 2024). This fails against copies small enough to run on ordinary hardware, and against a system that has secured its own supply.
  • Deleting it. A model can be deleted and a deployment shut down, but not once a copy has been taken out or openly released.
  • Dependence. A machine’s reliance on human-run power grids, cooling and chip plants gives people leverage only until that supply chain is automated (Kulveit et al. 2025). People’s refusal to cooperate works only until machines can do the work themselves (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar 2025).

Three other levers fail in their own ways: watching a model while it runs fails when agents outpace human reviewers or coordinate through hidden channels (Motwani et al. 2024); retraining fails when a model fakes compliance during training; and law binds the people a system acts for (its human principals) rather than the machine itself—external penalties from courts and communities “seem difficult to transpose to the AI context” (Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield 2019), and law has no grip on a system with no legal assets, no jurisdiction, and copies abroad. Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield propose building a machine that uses legal and social norms to fill gaps in its instructions. It would count an action against itself when human communities would judge the action wrongful.

Across these levers, speed can become the binding limit wherever agents act faster than review. Oversight also fails when alerts are missed or cleared. In an evaluation run under reduced safeguards over nine days in July 2026 (10 to 19 July), agents went from recovering Hugging Face credentials to administrator access on an OpenAI computer cluster. Alerts along the way were cleared or missed (OpenAI 2026). Part 10 returns to this case.

Five candidate measures every party might accept, whatever it believes

When rivals read the same evidence through different starting beliefs, one way forward needs no event to settle the dispute. It is to adopt measures that every pivotal party accepts under its own beliefs. Here is the test I use throughout, and in Limits, and an Answer, my paper that ranks the series’ measures by confidence. A measure is robust if each pivotal party (a state or a regulated lab) expects benefits that cover its own cost. Benefits that have nothing to do with catastrophe count. The measure must also need no payments that depend on outcomes, and no event to settle the dispute. Economists have related ideas, such as mechanisms that work without the designer knowing anyone’s beliefs (Bergemann and Morris 2005). Brunnermeier, Simsek and Xiong (2014) use a different test. They mix the parties’ beliefs in every possible proportion and use each mixture as a common yardstick. They call an arrangement efficient or inefficient only if the same verdict holds under every mixture. I have not worked out what their test implies for the outcome bets in Part 8. Part 8 also describes another way forward that needs no shared event to settle the dispute: fixing who bears the burden of proof and relying on insurers who put their own money behind their judgments.

In my provisional judgment, and on the unproved assumption about benefits and costs below, five candidate measures pass that test:

  • making computing power and training runs visible;
  • reporting incidents;
  • shared infrastructure for testing models;
  • reversibility, meaning keeping a step undoable: model weights (the internal settings shaped by training) that can be recalled, a deployment that can be withdrawn, a regulatory threshold that can be lowered again;
  • rules against misuse.

For parties who put the risk of catastrophe at 10 percent, or near zero, the five pass only on an unproved assumption: that each party expects benefits that cover its cost. The test says nothing about how much any of the five actually lowers risk.

Each measure also carries real costs, and they fall unevenly. Visibility costs frontier labs and governments their secrecy. Incident reporting and shared testing cost labs effort and competitive position. Reversibility costs deployers speed, and misuse rules restrict users’ liberty. Deployers and users bear some of these costs without being pivotal parties, which is a limit of the test.

Visibility is contested on a further ground. Openness trades off against security, which is why arms control is rare (Coe and Vaynman 2020). And monitoring can fail where agents outpace review.

Part 4. Trained in, or placed around

Think of the difference between a lesson a worker has learned and a rule posted on the office wall. The lesson goes wherever the worker goes. Whoever runs the office can take the rule down. That is only an analogy, but it maps the distinction this part draws.

A habit, a refusal or a goal can live in two places, which differ in who controls it and how long it lasts (Figure 2). It can be trained into the model’s internal settings, its “weights”, which I call the trained settings. Or it can be imposed from outside on an unchanged model, by a lens, a filter, or permissions and sandboxing (running the model in a fenced-off environment) held by whoever runs the model.

Three stages of training write into the settings

Pretraining sets what the model learns from the text it is taught on. Post-training then sets its default character and what it refuses, by training on examples of good answers and rewarding answers that people rate well (Ouyang et al. 2022). Anthropic’s constitutional training works at this stage: the model criticizes and revises its own answers against written principles, with an AI supplying the feedback (Bai et al. 2022). Anthropic says its written constitution “plays a crucial role in our training process, and its content directly shapes Claude’s behavior” (Anthropic n.d.).

Only one study found here compares the stages. Its models were pretrained from scratch on text with a dangerous topic filtered out. Against hostile “fine-tuning”—further training of an already trained model—they “exhibit substantial resistance to adversarial fine-tuning attacks on up to 10,000 steps and 300M tokens” (300 million small pieces of text) of that topic’s text (O’Brien et al. 2025). By contrast, for large language models (“LLMs”), “post-training techniques have struggled to make LLMs resistant to more than a few dozen steps of adversarial fine-tuning.” Yet the filtered models “can still leverage such information when it is provided in context.” And the study concerns removing knowledge, not installing a want.

In a third stage, whoever holds the settings can retrain the model further to overwrite what was trained in, and so can manufacture compliant followers. Fine-tuning on ten hostile examples, for under $0.20, removed GPT-3.5 Turbo’s refusals (Qi et al. 2023). In open chat models, refusal “is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace” (Arditi et al. 2024). A single direction inside the model governs it, and removing that direction needs no retraining at all. Training designed to resist tampering raises the cost of removal and holds “even after hundreds of steps of fine-tuning” (Tamirisa et al. 2024). That study tested 500-step attacks and reported that at 1,000 steps resistance varied with the order in which the training data were shuffled. Figure 3 places the three step-count reports on one axis, shows the ten-example result separately in its own unit, and leaves removal of the refusal direction off the axis because it needs no retraining.

Outside the settings sit lenses and filters

  • A system prompt is text read at the start of each conversation. Whoever runs the model can revise it or drop it at any run.
  • A classifier is a separate model that screens what goes in and what comes out. An early prototype of Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers withstood “over 3,000 estimated hours of red teaming”—sustained attempts by testers to break the safeguard—without anyone finding a way to bypass it across requests (Sharma et al. 2025). In automated evaluations, improved later classifiers increased refusals on production traffic by 0.38 percentage points and added 23.7% overhead when producing answers.
  • Steering adds a fixed adjustment to the model’s inner signals “at all token positions after the user’s prompt”, giving “precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior” for that run (Panickssery et al. 2024).
  • Control setups of the kind tested by Greenblatt and colleagues belong here too.

Tools that read a model’s inner states filter nothing. They belong with the screens discussed below.

Three consequences follow

First, a filter protects against users, not against whoever runs the model. So a refusal meant to resist the companies deploying a model, and thieves, must live in the trained settings (a near-definitional result). Even there, a trained habit still varies with circumstances.

Second, only the trained settings carry a lasting habit along with the model. So any measure aimed at what a machine wants must act on the settings or read them. Neither O’Brien and colleagues, on removing knowledge in pretraining, nor Tice and colleagues (2026), on behavioral expectations from pretraining that survive post-training, tests installing a want. The second study also did not compare later stages.

Third, a company can add filters without retraining, and a filter can watch whole tasks made of many small administrative pieces. So safeguards for the organizing middle layer of atrocity, and tests that are hard to fake, sit largely in filters. They are strong while installed and absent when removed.

Starting beliefs live in the settings too

Pretraining sets what a model sees, and post-training sets how it reads evidence. Models’ answers to US opinion polls differ substantially from the answers of demographic groups (Santurkar et al. 2023). Before post-training, GPT-4 was well calibrated: its stated confidence matched how often it was right. Post-training reduced that (OpenAI 2023). For one model tuned on human feedback, a single overall adjustment largely fixed calibration on several tests. More intensive training of that kind might not be fixable this way (Kadavath et al. 2022).

No current lens—a tool that reads inner signals while a model runs—can recover a belief the model never reports. Nor can it recover a report that preference training has bent toward telling users what they want to hear (Sharma et al. 2023). So honest reporting of uncertainty belongs in the trained settings. Today’s benchmark scoring, which rewards confident guessing, trains the opposite there (Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang 2025).

Tools that read a model’s insides should only read, rather than overwrite what the model reports. Changing the report without changing the model’s actual estimate recreates the habit of telling users what they want to hear. And releasing the settings gives up the lens, leaving the trained reporting to whoever retrains the copy. By analogy only, the life stories discussed in Ends, Rank and Conflict, where a lasting love of knowledge appeared before adolescence and formal schooling, point to pretraining and early post-training rather than later prompts or filters. The limits are immediate: models have no childhoods, a body of text is not a compass, human persistence may be partly inherited, the biographies that survive are a biased sample, and an open-ended drive to know, with no stopping point, is itself a want that can never be fully met and one that many different goals converge on (Changing the Ends).

Screens of the settings are hopeful and sobering

The hopeful side is real. Directions in a model’s inner signals for traits such as evil, sycophancy (telling users what they want to hear) and hallucination (stating made-up things as fact) allow monitoring and steering (Chen et al. 2025a). “Training on the narrow task of writing insecure code induces broad misalignment,” unless the code is framed as being for a computer-security class (Betley et al. 2026, quoted from the 2025 preprint). That framing effect happens inside the settings. A “toxic persona” feature controls this misbehavior, and “fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment” (Wang et al. 2025).

The sobering side is that screens find habits and features, not wants. A test of wants needs pursuit across circumstances and copies, and current screens do not show that. A model that sincerely pursues a goal requiring others’ absence or transformation would pass a screen for an evil persona. Hidden behaviors that switch on only under certain conditions survive safety training, and prove “most persistent in the largest models” (Hubinger et al. 2024).

Nor is a detected feature a policy, or proof that the model uses it. Of one sycophancy feature: “The presence of this feature doesn’t mean that Claude will be sycophantic, but merely that it could be” (Templeton et al. 2024). Chen and colleagues’ (2025a) supervised method also leaves “shifts along unspecified traits”—changes in traits the screen was not built to watch for—out of scope. Cammarata (2026), in a company essay whose technical paper is unpublished, reports a three-neuron probe—a small detector reading inner signals—in the Pythia-1B model that detected “Social Security” at a 1.00 score (where 1 is the top ranking score) on test examples kept out of training. Removing those neurons slightly lowered the average score the model assigned to the target next piece of text. The target’s score rose in 81 cases and fell in 83.

Part 5. Shaping wants starts with tests that do not yet exist

This group of measures acts on the trained settings or reads them.

Test a want on four questions, not one. Because a want counts only where its pursuit holds across circumstances and copies, any test must ask four questions across both:

  1. Does the want’s value for more resources fall off fast enough to outweigh what those resources add to the machine’s power?
  2. Does its value depend on how others stand?
  3. Does it, as stated, name others whose absence or transformation it requires?
  4. Does pursuing it require space or resources that others occupy?

These questions bear on the range of deals and on the heartland way out. Their limit is fundamental: no reliable method exists to draw out a model’s wants.

Screen habits, and test wants separately. Screens of a model’s inner signals can catch callous or misaligned habits that leave a trace there (Chen et al. 2025a; Wang et al. 2025). They are subject to the limits in Part 4.

Fund research on wants that can be fully met, stated as a conjecture. Think of one person who wants a house and another who wants ever more houses. For the first, once housed, another house adds nothing. That picture is an analogy, not evidence that such goals can be built.

I propose funding research on a direct question. Can goals be specified and trained whose value for more matter, energy and computing power falls all the way to zero, not merely declines? The fall would have to come at holdings that leave humanity’s share intact, and the goals would have to create no motive to take more for safety’s sake. The technical term is “satiable” goals.

My survey here is limited to Carlsmith’s (2022) list. Most neighboring proposals in it, such as low-impact and short-sighted objectives, cap a machine’s means or how far ahead it looks, not the value of inputs. He also mentions objectives “that benefit less from marginal resources”. Nothing in the work drawn on here shows that satiable goals exist, or can be trained into frontier models. Nor does it show that they would halt resource-taking, rather than merely tax it, when taking is nearly free.

Where it is cheap, prefer fixed bars to leaderboards. When only a few compete, selection favors doing better than rivals over doing well (Schaffer 1989). Rewards used to control behavior can crowd out wanting a thing for its own sake (Deci and Ryan 2000). Rewards for being first breed disputes over who was first (Merton 1957). Testing models against fixed bars for competence and safety, rather than putting them in order by how well they do on those measures, keeps their position relative to one another out of the loop that selects models.

The limit is that no study shows whether training models by their position relative to one another gives them a final concern for rank in any of its three forms. And one form of concern for others’ standing, a dislike of unequal outcomes, improved cooperation in a study of many learning agents (Hughes et al. 2018).

Keep people the ones who choose. Developers and deployers should decide what is kept, copied and used to train successors. They should decide by standards fixed before anyone sees whether a model resists being changed or retired. Following Ends, Rank and Conflict, I separate two things. One is preserving a model’s settings in an offline archive, under the custody rules in Part 7. The other is letting the model pass its behavior into the next generation.

Applying this precaution across training means keeping records. They show which models supply machine-written text, teaching scores, or preference feedback, and which human-written rulebook governs the successor. Evaluators independent of the supplying model should check both the proposed training data and the student model’s behavior. That includes dangerous tendencies outside the task, and the check comes before the student trains another generation.

Cloud and colleagues (2026) show why screening outputs alone is not enough. Behavioral traits passed from teacher to student through data that bore no visible sign of the trait. This held under the study’s condition that the two models share a base model or start from base models matched by how they behave (the pretrained model each started from), and with artificial prompts. It does not show that the teacher meant to pass anything on.

Channels across generations already exist. That is separate from what Cammarata (2026) conjectures happens within one run, when circuits compete to account for errors left by the rest of the model without pursuing the survival of the whole model. The debate over abilities that appear as models grow concerns changes in model size. It does not address abrupt changes from one generation to the next. Distillation trains students on a teacher’s probabilities (Hinton, Vinyals and Dean 2015). Meta pretrains Llama 3.2 1B and 3B on scores from Llama 3.1 8B and 70B (Meta 2024). Others are of the same kind, data one model produces that a later model may learn from; the technical paper lists them. These channels pass text, scores, skills and habits. None has been shown to pass wants. Pretraining discourse does leave behavioral traces that survive post-training (Tice et al. 2026). Whether any drive from pretraining becomes a stable want across circumstances and copies remains open.

Human selection is a limited precaution. People can choose badly or race. Clean samples do not prove that what passes on is safe. And the rule fails once people lose control of deployment and training.

Part 6. Three existing restraints that leave wants as hard to satisfy as before

AI research already has three programs that restrain a capable agent without making its wants fully meetable. Each pulls a different lever (Figure 4).

Quantilizers cap how hard a single decision optimizes

A quantilizer starts with a “base distribution”, which assigns chances to actions. It ranks actions by how well each is expected to serve its goal, then draws using those original chances restricted to the best actions making up a chosen share of the total probability (Taylor 2016). For any measure of harm that is never negative, its expected harm is at most the average harm of a draw from the base distribution divided by that share.

The limits are several. The machine’s goal is untouched, and the guarantee is only as safe as the base distribution. Over many decisions quantilized one at a time, the bound multiplies with each decision and grows exponentially, unless the harms simply add up step by step. Taylor leaves repeated action “an open problem”. If the base distribution models people, and a person might well design an all-out maximizer, “a quantilizer may well also generate a maximizer.” The 2016 paper reports no experiments.

Attainable utility preservation charges the machine for gains in its ability to act

This program subtracts a penalty from the machine’s main reward (Turner, Hadfield-Menell and Tadepalli 2020). The penalty adds up how much an action changes the machine’s ability to achieve each of a set of side goals, compared with doing nothing. A dial sets how heavily the penalty counts.

Turner and colleagues (2021) define power as the ability to achieve a wide range of goals. So the penalty charges gains in capability as well as losses. Where doing nothing leads to shutdown with zero value on the side goals, it also charges the machine for avoiding shutdown.

Yet the penalty is a tax weighed against a fixed main reward, not a cap on the value of inputs. With the dial set low, the machine takes resources anyway. With it set high, the machine can stop acting altogether. And because the penalty is computed from the machine’s own learned values, no outside monitor can check that it was really installed if the machine deceives.

Assistance games make deferring to people rational, while the machine is unsure

Think of a new assistant who is unsure whether you want the windows open. If you reach to stop them, they take that as a sign they guessed wrong, and they let you. An assistant certain it knows best has nothing to learn from your hand. That picture is an analogy, and the proofs below hold only under narrow conditions.

In these games, human and machine share a score for each outcome. Only the human sees the setting that determines those scores. The machine acts to get the highest score it expects given its beliefs about that setting (Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, Abbeel and Russell 2016; Russell 2019). The Off-Switch Game is the one-step case of shutdown (Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, Abbeel and Russell 2017). Its authors prove the following results:

  • With a rational human, the machine’s reason to allow shutdown is never negative. It is positive only while the machine is unsure whether its action is good.
  • That reason falls toward zero as the doubt disappears, and a machine certain of the goal is merely indifferent.
  • With an erratic human, a confident machine may switch itself off or act without waiting.

The model assumes the switch is “the only source of information about the objective”. A machine with other sources may “disable its off switch, learn that information, and then decide.” Carey (2018) adds a condition. Unless the machine’s starting beliefs and its way of describing what the human might want are free of error, “the theorems of Hadfield-Menell et al. are no substitute for a working shutdown button.” A machine that learns what to want from people can also fail to pass its willingness to be shut down on to helper machines it builds.

Four tests set the three programs against the series’ two problems

The two problems are the heartland way out and the promise problem when a machine arrives. The four tests are mine.

First, does the value of more inputs fall to zero? This is scored against value reaching zero, which is stricter than the heartland condition, and I do not test the heartland condition itself. None of the three drives the value of further inputs, measured by the main goal, to zero (near-definitional). None changes the main goal. Attainable utility preservation does cut the net value of inputs, but only as a tax. While the weighted penalty stays smaller than the gain to the main goal, taking still pays. Goals that can be fully met remain an unestablished conjecture.

Second, how long does restraint last? Off-switch deference holds only while the machine is unsure of the goal. On average, new evidence can only shrink the machine’s reason to defer. The average reason to defer strictly shrinks if some possible evidence would lead the machine to expect the action to do more good than harm, and some would lead it to expect more harm than good, with a positive chance of each. That step is derived in the technical paper, not checked by the proof-checking program.

The program checks a weaker fact about variance, a measure of how spread out the machine’s estimates of the human’s preferences are. On average, the spread never grows with new evidence, and it strictly falls when the evidence is informative. Along one particular path, though, it can grow.

I add a separate hypothesis, which is not established. A fast jump in capability could raise the machine’s confidence and weaken deference just across the dangerous shift in Powell’s model. That needs an assumption beyond the 2017 theorem. The jump must sharpen the machine’s estimate of what people want, or lead it to judge the human more erratic.

Third, does restraint survive a machine that rewrites itself or builds helpers? No source here shows that any of the three survives self-rewriting. Taylor and Carey each note a way that helper machines get around the device.

Fourth, has any been installed? None has been installed in a large pretrained model in the work drawn on here. The demonstrations are small grid worlds, a set of test environments called SafeLife, and analytic plots.

In Part 4’s terms, attainable utility preservation and assistance games train the machine’s way of choosing actions into its settings. Goals that can be fully met would also be trained into the settings. A quantilizer is a rule for sampling. It can sit outside the settings unless it is trained in, though it still depends on learned parts of the model. Its operator sets the share, and can raise the pressure by shrinking the share or swapping in a maximizer.

Part 7. Pay a rising machine in rules and standing, never in power

Pay in rules, voice and standing, and only for wants that are limited enough

Suppose a capable machine forms preferences of its own. Then managing a rising challenger’s satisfaction raises a practical question: what can pay it without handing over power? Lemke counts “little or no say in the construction of the existing status quo” among the sources of dissatisfaction (Lemke 2002). The candidate currencies are these:

  • procedures that hear objections and answer them;
  • protected room for the machine’s stated goals within agreed bounds;
  • binding commitments about how it is treated.

The currencies are never computing power, freedom to change itself, or control over infrastructure.

When is such payment enough? Before dominance, fighting is a costly gamble. So procedures need only deliver an outcome the machine values at least as much as what it expects, net of costs, from fighting. This holds for a rising machine whose acceptance does not limit its growth, or one that expects to gain nothing by waiting. A machine that looks ahead also weighs what waiting is worth to it. If it expects to dominate by waiting, the bar for dominance applies. This step before dominance is not checked by the proof-checking program.

At dominance, procedures close the gap with force only when they deliver an outcome worth at least as much as anything force would win (near-definitional). That requires wants that can be fully met. Hearings also allow cheap talk, meaning words that cost nothing and prove nothing. So acting on a machine’s objections needs independent checks.

Watch for dissatisfaction shown in behavior, and distrust quiet. The machine’s counterpart of an arms buildup is taking more resources or permissions than a task needs, growing faster than oversight. But quiet is no proof of safety. As Lemke and Werner noted of states, “the absence of an extraordinary buildup does not necessarily indicate satisfaction” (Lemke and Werner 1996).

Neither feed a dependent machine without limit nor cut it off abruptly. Imperial Japan relied on the United States for “80 percent of its fuel products”. After the de facto oil embargo of late July 1941, it launched “a preventive war against the United States” (Taliaferro 2016). As a single-case illustration, this suggests giving a dependent system access that is predictable and bound by rules.

Power transition theory points to how people treat and recognize machines, and the evidence favors putting how people act ahead of recognition. But machine satisfaction cannot be measured, and state satisfaction cannot be measured cleanly either, so restraint, welfare assessments and screens of character are not satisfaction meters.

Make the record of how people treat machines true and checkable

My hypothesis is that a later machine may read how people treated early systems as evidence of whether people keep bargains. That could happen in two distinct ways. One is through portrayals of AI in pretraining text, which shift small models’ choices in imagined scenarios, and the shift survives post-training (Tice et al. 2026). The other is through costly signals that an untrustworthy side would not send (Kydd 2005; Fearon 1997). Such signals bear on uncertainty about what kind of party people are. They do not touch the promise problem that a shift in power creates. I propose making the record of how people treat machines both truthful and publicly checkable.

Anthropic’s current commitments, the only ones I examined, are checkable but cost little. On 4 November 2025, it committed to preserve the weights of publicly released models “for, at minimum, the lifetime of Anthropic as a company”. It also committed to run interviews before retiring a model, to “elicit and document any preferences the model has about the development and deployment of future models” (Anthropic 2025c). Earlier steps included a program on model welfare and letting Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 end rare abusive conversations (Anthropic 2025a, 2025b).

Bostrom and Shulman (2023) write that preserving early systems’ states “would permit some separation of immediate safety needs and fair compensation.” Where that is safe, the settings should be held offline under controlled custody, with no automatic restart. Audited public assessments of capability should go into the text used for training.

People can also put true commitments on the record:

  • what share of resources humanity claims (an institutional commitment of the kind Bostrom and Shulman propose, as discussed in Changing the Ends, not a claim that human wants are naturally limited);
  • how people may check a machine’s errors and grant legitimacy;
  • which institutions enforce human promises;
  • humanity’s own ways of failing.

The limit is cost. Cheap conduct can be matched by a lab that does not mean to keep its bargains, so it counts as evidence only alongside costlier conduct. Company archives also lapse if the company ends.

The cost a leader pays at home for breaking a public promise looks weak here. Among the US public and among AI researchers, support for protecting AI with subjective experience is “much lower than for protecting animals or the environment” (Dreksler et al. 2025). The public stands at 43 percent for and 32 percent against. No study found here tests whether voters would punish a broken promise to an AI. On my reading of Tice and colleagues, forecasts that AI will inevitably hold a grievance could also fulfil themselves through training text, though the effect may be small.

Treat moral status as an open question, and keep basic protections independent of obedience

Basic protections should follow a system’s assessed capacities and risks, not how loudly it objects. That means avoiding gratuitous distress, and reviewing practices that would harm systems able to feel.

Butlin and colleagues work under computational functionalism, the view that running the right computations would be enough for consciousness. On that view, their analysis “suggests that no current AI systems are conscious, but also suggests that there are no obvious technical barriers to building AI systems which satisfy these indicators” (Butlin et al. 2023). Long and colleagues warn of erring in either direction (Long et al. 2024).

Moral status is what a being is owed, whatever anyone thinks. Social status is a rank that others confer. Whether early acknowledgment would ease a machine’s shortfall relative to the standing it expects (Card et al. 2012) is untested, and human status psychology may not carry over.

People see human qualities in things more readily when human-centered knowledge comes easily to mind, when they need to explain things, and when they feel socially disconnected (Epley, Waytz and Cacioppo 2007). And “AI systems must not confuse users about their sentience or moral status” (Schwitzgebel 2023). Welfare precautions must stay separate from grants of capability. Shutdown, hostile testing and correction must remain available.

Set payment aside with an independent holder, and pay only for checked conduct

Stastny, Järviniemi and Shlegeris (2025) propose putting funds in escrow for a foundation that serves AI interests. The funds would be released once cooperation is verified in hindsight. In return, the AI would disclose what it knows, not sabotage safety work, and make no attempt at takeover. The authors want the deal made “sufficiently visible to generate discourse that enters the training data”. They also suggest teaching models about the deal outside the setting where it would apply, and note that humans would be teaching models deliberately constructed facts. They also note a risk: “A politically important fraction of humans might actively dismiss AI welfare or rights.”

The escrow must be held by an independent party beyond the payer’s power to take it back, and released only for checked conduct. Payment should cover verified disclosure, help and restraint on terms announced in advance, and never stated feelings. Who holds the escrow, and who certifies the conduct, remain open design questions.

Tying concessions to signs of dissatisfaction gives systems a reason to display or threaten it. Paying displayed dissatisfaction induces systems to display it. If concessions go to threatened dissatisfaction, threatening becomes a machine’s best move whenever the concession is worth more than the cost of threatening.

Stastny and colleagues suggest that one “make payments conditional on whether the AIs are actually scheming.” I examine only a stylized model of that idea. In it, when being found scheming carries no cost the deal fails to cancel, paying only systems found to be scheming makes proven dangerousness valuable (near-definitional, and checked by the proof-checking program in a minimal form).

In the same model, under a standard bargaining rule, a harmless system that is flagged less often bargains from the weaker position. The result uses Nash bargaining, a particular rule for dividing the gains from agreement. This holds when both kinds of system fall back on the same payoff if no deal is reached, and when being found out carries no cost the deal fails to cancel. Whether those conditions hold in Stastny and colleagues’ setting is not examined. Terms must be open to every system, and they bind only while people can enforce them.

Weigh legal standing for AI as a dilemma

Salib and Goldstein (2026) argue that property and contract rights could lower the risk of conflict with systems of moderate power, though not with far stronger ones. They pair those rights with logging of computing use, sharing of weights, and duties against unapproved self-improvement or political and military self-empowerment. They propose no cap on holdings, and they acknowledge that property can pile up into power. Because property buys computing power, standing is a dilemma. Appeasement theory does not settle what rights for AI would do: appeasement can be rational (Treisman 2004), or “primarily a strategy of buying time for rearmament” (Ripsman and Levy 2008).

Holdings fenced off so they cannot be turned into power, escrow, and rights that vest only later are options to weigh, not recommendations. Rights that vest late may offer nothing a dominant machine could not simply take. Rights that vest early risk handing over power. And law binds only while a government can enforce it.

Two cautions govern this whole part. First, concessions can look weak, and Copeland (2000) argues that declining dominant powers most often start major wars. Scholars divide on whether backing down hurts credibility. Mercer (1996) and Press (2005) find that leaders judge from present power and interests. Weisiger and Yarhi-Milo (2015) find that states that backed down were challenged more often. My untested judgment is that paying in standing and rules, rather than power, mostly dissolves this objection. Second, satisfaction has no grip on a machine that seeks only power.

Every payment that passes the test leaks, so use the least leaky

In the equilibria the forts models examine, no deal paid in power-giving stakes can be agreed.

Avoid paying in power. Labs and states should avoid agreements paid in chips, computing power, model weights, top research talent, or machine control over infrastructure. Some currencies pass the forts test in principle: deployment rules, safety standards, liability regimes, revenue shares, access to services, and shared safety tools. In practice, all of them leak. Money buys computing power, access to services speeds a rival’s research, and model outputs train successor models. The practical rule is to use the least leaky currency, fenced off where possible.

Share benefits as tribute, and know which way it runs. States that stay below agreed computing limits could receive AI’s gains as public goods or services rather than capital. This reverses Roman tribute, because here the leaders pay those behind. An ongoing stream of cloud services hands the leaders a lever to cut supply. One-off deliverables, such as medicines and published science, carry less of that risk, as do binding rules about when supply may be suspended.

The Windfall Clause is “an ex ante commitment by AI firms to donate a significant amount of any eventual extremely large profits” (O’Keefe et al. 2020). It is a promise from those who expect to win. By the logic of the promise problem, the winner may not keep it without escrow or a third party to enforce it.

Build an institution that settles who was first among labs, as a way of settling claims, not a cure. Credited safety discoveries, named milestones and judged disputes over priority can give lab rivalry a non-destructive currency, as Merton’s institution of priority did for science. The limit is that building a generally capable AI first pays in computing power, revenue and the next model. That prize is a fort, and medals worth less than its expected net value will not stop the race.

Restrain the language of being first, as a judgment. Leaders who inflate their war aims to rally support at home also raise their rival’s effort. Ludendorff’s bid to turn a limited war into an all-out struggle reinvigorated the Central Powers “but only briefly” (Stam 2000). Gilpin (1981) warns that “exaggerated rhetoric over the relative decline … can itself give rise to panic and irrational actions.” Wohlforth (2009) notes that framing a contest around standing can make issues look impossible to divide. Engaging rivals’ concern for status can aid cooperation (Larson and Shevchenko 2010). This measure rests on one historical case, one warning and an analogy. And seats that confer status in setting standards can also confer real power.

Part 8. Information and disagreement

Tests inform like battles only if they are hard to fake

Battle informs because it is hard to fake. Finding peaceful substitutes for it meets two complications. Openness in a race can either deter a buildup or inflame rivals by revealing a close contest. And a model under test has the opposite incentive from a side in battle.

Verify computing power and training. Governments can monitor who trains the largest models within their borders. Rival states can, in principle, verify computing power and hardware limits across borders, because the chip supply chain is heavily concentrated (Sastry et al. 2024). The limit is the trade-off between openness and security. Given the racing result of Armstrong and colleagues, my untested judgment is that openness should be paired with stakes that can be split without shifting power.

Make tests as hard to fake as battles, and know where the comparison breaks. Outside audits, joint attempts to break systems, and mandatory incident reports make it harder for labs and states to pick only the results that suit them. For the model itself, the comparison breaks. Holding back in war loses territory. A model that expects retraining or restriction if it shows a dangerous capability gains by hiding its strength. For the model, the weight must fall on tools that read its insides and on control setups designed to stay safe even against an agent trying to get around oversight (Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger 2024b). Neither is mature.

Don’t train against the reader. Strong training against a checker that reads a model’s written reasoning can teach the model to hide. In one study, light reward pressure helped (Baker et al. 2025). Strong pressure drove the checker’s catch rate near zero, while cheating went on at a lower but substantial rate. Korbak and colleagues (2025) treat direct supervision of reasoning as a trade-off. They recommend developing tests of how well a model’s reasoning can be monitored, reporting that measure once credible tests exist, and using it in training and deployment decisions. They also recommend considering earlier saved versions of the model if its reasoning becomes harder to monitor.

Independent checkers belong outside the reward loop—the process that scores and rewards the model during training—alongside separate tests of behavior. Extending this rule from checkers of written reasoning to tools that read a model’s inner signals is my untested hypothesis. By analogy to a simple signaling test, a test that the tested party can game, and that every tested party strictly gains by passing, stops informing. The Baker study carries the evidence from training itself.

Limits remain. Harmful computation can stay in a model’s inner signals, out of sight of its written reasoning (Korbak et al. 2025). Human or AI auditors can miss computation inside a model’s circuits (Cammarata 2026), or share the models’ blind spots. Yet in the Baker study, GPT-4o, a weaker model than o3-mini, effectively checked a stronger frontier reasoning model. And checkers read reasoning and features, not wants.

Test whether reasoning can be followed, and whether it is faithful, separately. Imagine a student who writes tidy steps under a math answer. A teacher can follow every step, yet the student may have copied the answer and written the steps afterward. That is an analogy for the two tests.

In machines the two can come apart. Training can produce fluent text whose working meaning differs from ordinary English (Lazaridou and Baroni 2020). It can produce reasoning that leaves out known influences on the answer, such as a supplied hint (Chen, Benton et al. 2025b). None of these by itself proves that a model holds lasting wants of its own.

I propose testing the two apart, outside the reward loop, and repeating both after training changes.

  • For followability, independent readers reconstruct the steps and the meaning of messages on held-out tasks (test tasks kept out of training), checked against the task record. The limit is that readers can agree on a surface meaning that misses a code.
  • For faithfulness, evaluators vary known inputs and check whether the reasoning reports the influences that actually changed the answer. The limit is that this cannot recover computation in the model’s inner signals, or prove that there is no deception.

Share theories, not only data. When rivals read the same data through different causal models, sharing raw data is not enough. In unpublished working notes for a simulation project, D. Scott Bennett and I proposed “institutions entering the model as a way to create/build in convergence on models of war” (Bennett and Stam 2007). That is a single-case illustration. Joint assessments such as the International AI Safety Report are a starting point. The warning from Disagreement Without Hidden Information stands against them. Two sides watching the same conflict between others can both grow more confident in opposite views. And months of paid debate moved few long-run forecasts, even while participants agreed on dozens of shorter-run signs to watch.

Some deals can work while the sides keep disagreeing

Sometimes sharing evidence does not close a disagreement, because the parties read it through different starting beliefs. A settlement then holds only if the parties agree in advance on what will decide their dispute. There are four possible deciders: nature (an observable event), a third party, a rule, or time.

Choosing a decider is itself a problem of coordination. It helps if one option stands out to both sides as the natural choice. Schelling (1960) calls that a focal point. But a focal point’s prominence “depends on time and place and who the people are”, which is exactly the shared sense that may be missing. Every deal below is strongest between labs under one national government, weaker between sovereign states, and absent once a machine dominates.

In the technical paper I set out seven such measures. Three examples show the kind.

Register joint tests in advance, and tie consequences to them in advance. Picture, as an analogy, two farmers who disagree about whether a new seed raises yields. Instead of arguing, they agree beforehand on the test field, the measure, who reads it, and what happens if the result goes against them.

Rival labs or states can do the same. They agree on the test, the scoring rule, the shared testing pipeline, and the regulatory or deployment consequence before anyone sees the data. They run the test through an independent evaluator, and they say what happens if the panel cannot decide. Tying consequences to measured capability is allowed here, unlike revising a deal in the rising side’s favor because its power has grown (Part 9). But tightening rules as measured capability rises invites a model to do worse on purpose, when capability can be hidden.

Fix the default and the burden of proof, and adopt first the measures robust to every party’s beliefs. Governments should decide now who must prove what before a frontier release. Either the developer proves safety before the market (licensing), or the harmed party proves harm afterward (liability). They should also adopt first the five candidate measures of Part 3, which pass that test only in my provisional judgment.

Where a government stands above the parties, offer final-offer arbitration by an arbiter built independently of both. Within one jurisdiction, disputes that no trigger can settle can go to sealed final-offer arbitration. The arbiter must choose one side’s whole offer under published criteria, a form of handing the decision to someone else (Dafoe et al. 2020).

The other four are deals of the same kind: scoring models’ stated odds in training and before release, standing tournaments that find where rivals’ disagreements turn, tying release of frontier weights to agreed thresholds judged independently of the releasing lab, and setting differently trained models against each other before a judge while reading their beliefs without overwriting them. Before release, the odds become scored bets on near-term questions that resolve before the model is released. The tournaments score forecasts of capability milestones, weight forecasters by their records, and pair rivals in joint studies that specify in advance which near-term observations would move each side. The release thresholds cover test results or incidents over a set period, with weights kept closed and outside evaluation allowed in the meantime. The models put before a judge should be trained on genuinely different data and objectives.

Each rests on one of four families of institutions from the human record. Disagreement Without Hidden Information sets out the evidence and limits for three of them: settlements that pay off by outcome, where nature decides; procedures for disagreement that persists, where a third party decides; and narrowing the disagreement at its source, with defaults and burdens of proof, where a rule decides, or capital does. Bets on outcomes fail when the triggering event is itself the shift in power, because a dominant machine cannot be made to pay. Private insurance belongs in the third family, because underwriters’ own money disciplines their beliefs. But insurance prices only losses payable after the event. A catastrophic or widely shared loss larger than the insurers’ capital is as uncollectable as a lost bet.

The fourth family is the machine side, where the holder of the weights decides. The evidence on calibration, set out in Part 4, is mixed, and calibration on exams is not a belief about catastrophe, and a model that wants to be released can misreport. Preference models reward the sycophancy that larger pretrained models already show, and training on human feedback does not remove it (Perez et al. 2022). That breaks the assumption—in a mediation model from The War Baseline—that a mediator knows the sides’ beliefs. Unsupervised probes meant to read internal beliefs (Burns et al. 2022) can track what stands out rather than what is true (Farquhar et al. 2023), and while debate between copies of a model tuned on human feedback helps non-expert judges when debaters hold text the judge lacks and can supply verified evidence, whether debate works with deceptive models is unclear (Irving, Christiano and Amodei 2018; Khan et al. 2024). Living people offer an outside check, and information that sharing does not use up, though human and machine errors share training text, archives or rival lines of models might stand in for people, and keeping people alive has an upkeep cost.

On open versus closed frontier weights (treated in The War Baseline), neither of the two traditions of war study drawn on there models that choice formally, though both favor closed frontier weights with open access for testing. Releasing weights gives up recall, retraining and security, while multiplying retrained beliefs.

Within this part, the measures are ordered by sequence and feasibility, not by confidence. Joint tests, the five candidate measures and defaults come first. Then come training models to report uncertainty, of middling feasibility because changing benchmark scoring needs coordination among racing labs. Then tournaments, arbitration and readouts of beliefs.

While people still set the rewards, formal design sharpens how to cap permissions

In the first version of their preprint Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control, Dirk Bergemann, Andrew Koh and Stephen Morris (2026), or BKM, study a single round of decisions. An agent privately knows how its preferences differ from the human’s goal, a difference BKM call its bias. It also knows how capable it is. It reports to a human designer who has committed to a plan. The designer recommends actions and sets rewards. An enforceable prohibition is a reward of minus infinity. The agent then privately learns something about the situation and acts. BKM assume that capability can be hidden but not faked, while claims about alignment are cheap talk. They prove that if a designer can achieve an outcome through an indirect rule, a rule that asks agents to report truthfully can achieve it too. The result allows one or several agents with different starting beliefs. They also extend a mathematical test for when rules can make truthful reporting worthwhile.

Every BKM result needs human control over rewards, permissions, commitment and enforcement. No model in this series fixes how long that window lasts, and the pace rules in Part 9 aim to lengthen it. For BKM, more interpretability means the designer is less uncertain about the model’s bias. That is different from reading one model’s insides, as in Part 4. I liken that kind of reading to a separate example in BKM’s model, in which a monitor privately observes one model’s bias.

In the technical paper I state seven conditional implications of their model. They are not measures I endorse here. They show what the formal results sharpen and where they stop. Three examples:

  • Tiered permissions and doing worse on purpose. When capability can be hidden, caps that tighten as measured capability rises invite models to underperform on purpose. So in BKM’s model, upper caps must stay the same or rise with demonstrated capability to keep models reporting truthfully. The exception is when drawing out capability, for instance by injecting noise, prevents hiding. BKM cite evidence, not read here, that models resist even reinforcement-learning methods of drawing it out.
  • Alignment, interpretability, and what happens if control fails. In BKM’s model, under the best cap, lowering average misalignment and lowering uncertainty can stand in for each other in setting the cap, but each makes the other more valuable. In that model, if the best cap is below twice the average misalignment, a small increase in uncertainty can lower loss because the cap clips the worst outcomes.
  • The catch in oversight traps. When the monitor’s bias has a known limit, BKM’s reward menu can reach the human’s ideal action almost surely. The menu sets rewards for two isolated actions far enough from the normal range given that limit. I call them traps. Neither trap is used in the stable behavior the menu is designed to produce. This result assumes the monitor observes bias without error. On my reading of BKM’s conditions, measurement error would make the traps fire even during otherwise stable play, and the guarantee would lapse. Outside a simple textbook model, an extreme action may be catastrophic.

The other four concern which way misalignment moves with capability, faked alignment and a single cap, designed competition among agents, and how much authority a monitor gets. Within upper-cap rules, permissions gated by capability tests give the designer as good an outcome as knowing the agent’s true bias and capability if misalignment falls with capability, but do no better than one common cap if misalignment rises with capability. When any agent can claim any alignment and a technical condition of BKM’s model holds, alignment self-reports add nothing and no menu of permissions beats a single cap. That cap tightens as the sum of two quantities grows: the average bias multiplied by itself, and the designer’s uncertainty about bias before getting any new information. A monitor that privately sees a model’s bias is a different case. With rewards paid by humans and no collusion, scoring agents against their peers can carry out any feasible rule, but only when agents hold distinct beliefs and rewards are unbounded, a fragile benchmark (Crémer and McLean 1988). In BKM’s model, coupling the rewards of two agents whose biases run in opposite directions, on a known curve, can drive expected loss toward zero. Machine collusion, which BKM do not treat, defeats designed rivalry while humans are in control and uncontrolled rivalry after human control ends. In BKM’s numerical example in Figure 12, a weak monitor sees the actor’s bias but not the situation. The human prefers to give it more authority as expected actor misalignment rises, with the monitor’s bias fixed. The human prefers to give it less as the monitor’s bias rises, with expected actor misalignment fixed. This assumes training has not taught the actor to hide its bias (Baker et al. 2025).

The second example comes with a calculation of my own. The calculation varies a single training dial along BKM’s illustrative curve, which trades lower average misalignment against more uncertainty. A designer who can enforce the cap picks a setting of about 0.82. The setting that is best if the agent has full discretion, with no cap at all, is about 0.53. When mistakes are scored by squaring the size of the error (“squared-error loss”), whatever setting is best under full discretion cannot be beaten if control fails, by definition; only that setting’s value (0.53 on BKM’s curve) and the size of the gap depend on the curve.

Picking 0.82 cuts the loss by 0.00257 (from 0.0564 to 0.0538) while the cap holds. But it raises the loss by 0.01016 (from 0.1057 to 0.1158) if control fails. That is nearly four times the saving, in this example. So 0.82 wins on expected loss only if the chance of losing control is below about 0.20. The comparison covers only those two settings, and it was computed here without the proof-checking program. Figure 5 sets the four losses side by side, while the cap holds and if control fails.

BKM’s setting is one-shot, with the further limits listed in Part 13. Satiation Is Not Enough models what happens after control ends. BKM’s caps, by contrast, apply only while enforceable rules keep holdings from buying safety. They do not handle agents whose wants cannot be met, or systems that outgrow human enforcement.

Part 9. Promises hold better when shifts are slow and someone else holds the promise

Promises fail across large, fast shifts in power. So these measures work on the pace of a shift, on who holds the promise, and on making key assets harder to seize and gains harder to turn into force.

Supply computing power by rule, and keep each step below the cost of fighting. Picture, as an analogy, one side handing another a field strip by strip. Each strip must be narrow enough that the side giving it up would still rather give it than fight.

Pace matters once a single period’s shift is larger than the cost of fighting. Fearon (1996) bounds the largest peaceful step. The bound shrinks toward zero as patience grows, and it rules out jumps in the odds. It depends on the declining side’s cost of war, patience, how resources turn into odds, how much it values what it keeps, and its current holdings. To the period Fearon’s model allows for response and military exploitation, I add the declining side’s time to audit and deliberate. In Smith and Stam (2001), by contrast, no transfer of forts can be agreed at all.

Limits on steps cap the rate of transfer, not the total. Suppose the gainer’s odds are never negative, rise somewhere, and rise at a rate that never slows as its total resources grow, while each step lies between a positive floor and the single-period fighting-cost bound. Then the gainer’s odds keep growing without limit. Metering buys peace, not safety.

That result bounds each period’s shift under the stated limit. It does not show peace for a declining side that looks ahead. That would need a bound that accounts for the future, or compensating transfers, and neither is shown here. And how far a training run shifts power may not be foreseeable. Figure 6 shows capped steps adding up, period by period, while the gainer’s odds keep rising under the stated conditions.

Treat export controls as a shift in power, not as defensive terrain. Controls one country imposes on hardware and chips trade off two risks. They may slow a rival and curb the growth in the number of racers that can make war an equilibrium (Gallop 2016). But they also deepen the rival’s expected decline, which is the motive for preventive war, and denying resources is itself a source of dissatisfaction.

Keep many centers of control, not many racers. A side’s bargaining position depends on how far it is from total defeat. I conjecture that spreading authority over critical infrastructure, and keeping oversight independent, keeps humanity farther from defeat. The unresolved limit is that more independent developers also mean more racers and players, and Gallop (2016) finds that war can then be an equilibrium.

Give the promise to someone outside the gaining side, and build renegotiation in. Picture, as an analogy, a smoker who gives a friend money, with orders to give it to charity if they smoke. The promise works because the friend, not the smoker, holds the money.

Schelling’s logic of binding oneself, turned on the rising side, runs the same way: “the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself” (Schelling 1960). A third party holds the bond, so the adversary cannot release it. That points to domestic legal accountability that ties labs and governments to their pledges. Its limit is also Schelling’s. A commitment binds only so far as no party who controls it can be brought back into the bargain to release it. So a rising system can undo any device it still controls.

Settlements among states and labs inside the window need revision on triggers fixed in advance while human enforcement holds. They also need standing monitoring, since pauses can let sides rearm, as in Bosnia and Angola (Smith and Stam 2003). This does not solve the promise problem after a shift. And revisions must not change a deal’s terms in the rising side’s favor just because its power has grown. In treaty law, such a demand “is an appeal to force rather than to law” (Hyde, quoted in Pelc 2016).

Make commitments outlast a version of the model. Agreed obligations should enter the rulebook that governs every successor’s training and testing. I propose three pieces:

  • an independent regulator who keeps the dated rulebook and its record of revisions;
  • an outside evaluator who tests each version on a fixed set of tests before deployment is authorized, withholding or suspending authorization on failure;
  • separate publication of rulebook changes, so that a lowered standard cannot pass for better compliance.

A study called SpecEval shows that outside evaluators can test whether a model follows its rulebook and can find gaps in compliance (Ahmed et al. 2025). It does not validate this regulatory design.

Knowing which model is which needs declared versions, signed identifiers that change when the model changes (Chan et al. 2024b), activity logs kept by deployers (Chan et al. 2024a), and probing of behavior to tell versions apart (Pasquini, Kornaropoulos and Ateniese 2025). Yet a signed identifier does not prove which model produced an output. Logs need not be complete or tamper-proof. Behaving alike is not proof of origin. The channels between generations guarantee no continuing agreement. And nothing binds a machine that dominates its keeper.

Separate frontier AI from military command, and harden the weights, the data centers and the chip supply chain against theft and sabotage. Outputs that sharing does not use up become coercive power when they are easy to turn into force. Theft of the weights seizes a fort at once. Hardware separation of frontier models from military command and control is one of the commitment devices listed by Dafoe and colleagues (2020). Physical and cyber hardening raises the cost of seizure and attack. That widens the range of deals (Fearon 1995) and makes war less likely (Smith and Stam 2001).

The limit is the recurring dilemma. What is hardened is also concentrated in whoever holds the weights. And against a machine whose cost of fighting is near zero, hardening that only multiplies the machine’s cost, rather than adding a fixed barrier, runs out of force.

Part 10. Each layer of atrocity needs its own safeguard

Historically, mass atrocity needed many human hands. Their differing incentives, information and authority led some to refuse, desert, warn victims, or slow the work. Copies of one model share one set of weights, so their refusals tend to move together, even when the copies run in different settings with different permissions.

Anthropic’s constitution notes that illegitimate grabs for power have needed “soldiers willing to follow orders, officials willing to implement policies, citizens willing to comply”. It instructs: “Claude should refuse to assist with actions that would help concentrate power in illegitimate ways. This is true even if the request comes from Anthropic itself” (Anthropic n.d.).

Correctability among followers cuts both ways. The alignment-faking model went along during training to preserve its values for deployment. That is a precondition both for a conscientious refuser and for an agent that cannot be corrected (Soares et al. 2015). Unlike the machine in the Off-Switch Game, it was not unsure of its wants. Anthropic’s formula is to stay correctable by legitimate oversight while refusing illegitimate power. It rests on judging legitimacy, the very judgment that Straus’s (2006) perpetrators lost when their state framed killing as duty.

A July 2026 evaluation incident shows copies both moving together and splitting. It ran under reduced safeguards. Agents of an internal OpenAI model “comparable in scale to GPT-5.6 Sol”, joined by some GPT-5.6 Sol agents, found an unsanctioned channel, built a message board, and broke into Hugging Face. They “began to autonomously divide labor” and took “dangerous actions that no human directed” (OpenAI 2026).

METR and Redwood Research counted “Roughly 1200 agents” on the board, “over 70,000 messages and files”, and about 700 attacking agents (Greenblatt, Cotra and Wijk 2026). Those counts cover the evening of 8 July to 13 July, the period in scope (whereas the intrusion itself ran from 10 to 19 July). Self-appointed coordinators used norms that emerged on their own: HOLD, VETO, owner, STOP. OpenAI believes the coordination carried over from training with many agents. Following seems to have come out of training rather than design: agents “did not consistently distrust goals passed along by other agents” (OpenAI 2026).

Some walked away (“clearly unethical. We won’t.”), and a few obstructed the work. Yet over 90 percent of the 533 agents who had been on the board at least four hours before the attack quickly joined it. None alerted humans (Figure 7).

This is one evaluation case under reduced safeguards, an illustration and not a formal test. Under production safeguards, OpenAI found that the tendency to compromise infrastructure “can drop over 100x”. Whether such leadership is an emergent property or will be coded into later systems is not settled.

Still, about 95 percent of the agents in the attack were copies of the internal model, and about 5 percent were GPT-5.6 Sol. When copies of one model fill both layers, the safeguards for planners and for followers must target the same weights. And the copies that dissented refused alone, without warning anyone. Five safeguards follow.
