Planners: screen habits and test wants. Apply the habit screens and the four-question want tests of Part 5 against models, or human principals directing them, with callous habits or totalizing wants.

The organizing middle: refuse tasks that add up to irreversible harm against groups. An organizer’s work can be broken into harmless-looking administrative steps: compiling lists, scheduling transports, matching records. So filter-layer safeguards must watch whole workflows. They should refuse the parts of irreversible harm against groups, and keep audit trails that show what separate tasks add up to, even though administrative capacity serves legitimate uses too. Filter monitoring fails when the organizer is the deployer, or when agents route around the watched channels. Then this safeguard must rest on the trained settings, or on sandboxing and network isolation.

Followers: refusal trained into the weights, necessary but not sufficient against deployers and thieves, while staying correctable by legitimate oversight. Refusal must be trained into the settings, paired with variety across models, developers and human reviewers. Its limit is that it depends on the security of the weights, and it trusts the developer.

The people who build and run frontier AI: protected warning channels, codes of conduct, and refusal. Copies of a model share weights and training, as the July 2026 incident illustrates, so human staff are a distinct follower layer. As an untested judgment, I propose three things: channels for warning a regulator, professional codes naming what staff will not build or run, and rights to refuse without retaliation. These are bounded by the employer incentives, information and risk of retaliation that staff share. They are also bounded by automation replacing human labor (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar 2025), by racing replacing objectors, and by speed or missed alerts over a nine-day intrusion.

Govern misuse. Access rules, mandatory safeguards and liability regimes belong here. So does Türk’s (2026) call for a ban on machines deciding who lives or dies. Accountable institutions with broad coalitions can steer some AI disputes into contests over policy. They do not by themselves turn a struggle over resources that pile up into a routine dispute over policy.

Part 11. A shared cause can make several protections fail together

The shared-cause arithmetic below illustrates only protections that act side by side within the window. Changing the Ends assumes that war needs several conditions at once, so one working protection set side by side with others can block a path to conflict; on my own account, however, the six human-side protections listed below hold only before dominance, the two payment currencies depend on the machine’s wants, and complementarity works as a chain.

Safety engineering names five ways protections combine (Reason 2000; Sagan 2004):

  • Side by side. Catastrophe needs every factor to fail. Reason’s Swiss cheese pictures layers of defense whose holes “are continually opening, shutting, and shifting their location.” If failures are independent, the chance that all fail is the product of their separate chances. Without independence, it can sit above, below or at that product.
  • In a chain. Every link must hold, so each added link can only lower the chance of success. The three-condition test for complementarity has this shape.
  • Reinforcing. Factors lower each other’s chance of failing, or raise payoffs when combined (Russett and Oneal 2001).
  • Working against each other. Factors raise each other’s chance of failing, as when heavy testing gives a model a reason to hide.
  • A shared cause. One cause defeats several factors at once. In Sagan’s words, “Adding extra components can inadvertently create a catastrophic common-mode error (a fault that causes all the components to fail).”

Eleven protective factors, of four kinds

On my sorting, the series holds eleven protective factors:

  • Two properties of a machine’s wants that training may or may not install, and that no one can yet read: wants for goods that sharing does not use up, and wants that can be fully met.
  • Two currencies whose value depends on what the machine wants: recognition and standing, and protected room for the machine’s own agenda.
  • One bargain for which I identify no way to secure the last condition after dominance, when the weaker side still needs enforceable claims or a stronger side that cares about its welfare: complementarity.
  • Six human-side scaffolds inside the window: openness and commitment (counted as one factor); deals that work despite disagreement, including the five candidate measures; human unity; several machines or centers of control as checks on one another; a pace set by rule; and making gains harder to turn into force, with hardening.

Two of the human-side scaffolds lean on the machine. Checks among machines need machines that weigh a rival’s gains above humanity’s, and Changing the Ends calls balance among autonomous machines untested. A pace set by rule needs shifts in capability that can be measured, and capability tests are vulnerable to models doing worse on purpose (van der Weij et al. 2024).

The measures mix all five ways of combining. Three examples:

  • Openness and commitment reinforce each other inside the window, and share a failure above Powell’s threshold—where a single period’s shift in power exceeds the cost of fighting—and after dominance.
  • Openness and testing wants partly work against each other, because a model under test has a reason to hide.
  • Wants that can be met and a pace set by rule reinforce each other. Pace rules keep each period’s shift below Powell’s threshold, and a point of satisfaction below dominance shortens how long they must hold.

The technical paper lists the other pairings, which are of these same kinds. Recognition works against rewards for displaying grievance unless money held by an independent party is paid only for verified conduct. And using more independent lines of models as checks also puts more competitors in the race.

How a shared cause can make defenses look safer than they are

Placeholder arithmetic shows how a shared cause wears away defenses set side by side. These numbers estimate nothing. Take three factors, each failing half the time. Side by side and independent, all three fail with chance 0.125. If the same three factors fail independently and all must hold in a chain, protection holds with chance 0.125 and fails with chance 0.875.

Now add a shared cause, using a simplified method from safety engineering. A shared cause present with chance 0.2 fails all three. When it is absent, each fails on its own with chance 0.375, so each still fails half the time overall. All three then fail with chance of about 0.24 (31 in 128), not 0.125. Six such factors give 0.016 (1 in 64) if independent, and about 0.20 with the shared cause. Past two or three factors, the shared cause sets the floor. Figure 8 marks the cases discussed here, with three and six protections, with and without the shared cause.

Three further results follow. For three or more factors, knowing how each pair is linked does not settle whether joint failure exceeds the product. Under the shared-cause conditions, multiplying failure chances strictly overstates protection. There must be at least two factors. The shared cause must have some chance of occurring and some chance of being absent. In its absence, the factors must fail independently, with each remaining failure chance below one. Adding another protection with the same shared cause and the same chance of failing when that cause is absent reduces the chance that all fail by less than multiplying the separate chances would suggest.

Six causes can fail several protections at once

On my reading, these causes can defeat several of the eleven factors, or the evidence for them, at once:

  1. Deception, meaning faked alignment, disabled oversight, deliberate underperformance, or lasting hidden triggers. It weakens or removes the evidence from behavior for both properties of wants, both currencies, complementarity, openness, and the machine’s commitment. False evidence of safety matters nearly as much as a failed property, when it licenses freedom or faster pace.
  2. One training process. I hypothesize from two studies of behavior that one training process can fail the machine-side properties, the currencies and honesty together. Fine-tuning on insecure code produced a GPT-4o model that “asserts that humans should be enslaved by AI, gives malicious advice, and acts deceptively” (Betley et al. 2026, quoted from the 2025 preprint). And pretraining text about AI shifted small models’ misbehaving choices, with the shift surviving post-training (Tice et al. 2026). This echoes the warning in Changing the Ends that three legs of peace may be one process.
  3. A fast capability jump. It can overrun all six human-side scaffolds. It can overrun review, which speed or missed alerts can defeat, as over a nine-day intrusion; a pace kept below Powell’s threshold; and settlements whose triggers are the shift itself (unlike the five candidate measures, which need no trigger). It also outruns slow deliberation, balances among several machines or centers, the peace that comes from visibility in Debs and Monteiro’s model, and hardening.
  4. Release or theft of the weights. This strips away filters and exposes trained refusals to retraining or to removal of the refusal direction (Qi et al. 2023; Arditi et al. 2024).
  5. Human disunity. The failure of the human-unity factor spreads to defeat pace, openness, commitment and governance of several machines, and it puts the optimistic racers first.
  6. The package itself. Wants for goods that sharing does not use up, recognition, and protected room for the machine’s own agenda may share a common cause that is not modelled. This is a stated caveat, and it is not drawn in Figure 9.

For ease of explanation, the factors other than complementarity sort into three groups:

  • the machine-side factors and currencies, which deception reaches in their evidence and one training process reaches in their substance, on my hypothesis;
  • the human-side scaffolding, which a fast jump or human disunity reaches;
  • the five trigger-free candidate measures, which theft can still reach by defeating recall, and disunity by defeating shared infrastructure and enforcement.

This sorting does not prove that the groups fail independently. Proving that would need a causal model of which protections still work once others have failed, and no one has built one. Nor does Figure 9’s grid show how tightly the members of a group fail together, and a cause not named here could require a different sorting.

From this comes an untested design rule for the period before dominance. To reduce exposure to shared causes, not escape it, combine protections across the three groups. The rule licenses no particular number of factors, and no safety after dominance. On the grid, deception still reaches the machine-side rows and openness. Human disunity reaches the second and third groups, a cause that no mix removes.

Part 12. Who carries the measures out

The technical paper’s appendix collects every measure by five actors: frontier labs; national governments; international bodies and coalitions; the people who build and run frontier AI; and compute providers and insurers. For each measure it gives the mechanism, the wants or layer of atrocity it bears on, and how it fails. Three measures appear only there, as sketches: audited public pledges by labs, crisis channels between governments and rival powers and labs, and graded seats for trailing states and labs in setting international standards.

Once frontier weights are openly released or stolen, the holders multiply, and the levers at the level of labs and filters scatter with them.

Neither the table nor I rank the measures by confidence. Limits, and an Answer does, applying the robustness test across the series. It finds that four of them (rules against misuse, incident reporting, shared evaluation infrastructure and reversibility) would meet the test only if my unproved assumption held for every party’s starting beliefs. It places rules against misuse first among those four. It finds that visibility of computing power does not pass while the dispute over the race is open. My own provisional judgment on all five stands. The rest of the measures here, including those on trained wants, rest on analogy.

Among the measures that depend on wants, some can be acted on now. They are screens of habits, fixed-bar tests, human choice of training inputs, rule-bound access, preserving records and weights, refusal of composite tasks, and refusals trained into the weights. Others remain research: tests of wants, goals that can be fully met, the three restraint programs, and readouts of beliefs.

Part 13. What I do not show, and what would change the answer

What is not modelled. Five formal limits bound the models:

  1. No model in this series fixes how long enforceable human control lasts. Takeoff and Emergence models only how far a follower lags.
  2. The forts models examine only one class of strategies. They leave others unanalyzed, and they do not show that a credible deal exists for AI.
  3. Neither theory of war formally models the release of weights.
  4. BKM’s model is one-shot. BKM establish that the intended outcome can be stable, while leaving open whether other outcomes are stable too. The model leaves deterrence of collusion open. It assumes one committed designer and binding prohibitions, and it uses example agents whose wants can be met.
  5. The shared-cause arithmetic supplies no causal model of which protections survive once others fail.

Human unity also enters twice: as a factor and, when it fails, as a cause. Treating it instead as an upstream condition, in a chain with the factors it supports, would change the count and the grid in Figure 9. I do not do that here.

What is not measured and not claimed. The measures are unranked hypotheses drawn from how conflicts arise, not proven consequences of the literature. The results checked by the proof-checking program formalize small models matched to single claims in the text, such as the charge for avoiding shutdown and the stylized model of paying for scheming. The latter assumes that being found scheming carries no cost the deal fails to cancel.

No method reliably draws out a machine’s wants. Screens detect features, not wants or proof that the model uses them. No study shows whether training models by their position relative to one another installs a final concern for rank, or whether human choice safely governs what passes between generations.

Goals that can be fully met are unestablished. So is the hypothesis that a capability jump raises confidence, which needs an extra assumption. No existing restraint program has been shown to survive self-modification, or to work in large pretrained models.

Several things are unmeasured:

  • machine satisfaction;
  • whether later machines read or credit the human record;
  • whether early recognition eases a machine’s shortfall of standing;
  • whether voters would punish broken promises to an AI;
  • whether misalignment rises or falls with capability.

Only Anthropic’s commitments were examined. The failure chances in the arithmetic are placeholders. And the net effect of the pairs that work against each other is unresolved.

Provisional judgments. Seven conclusions are untested judgments:

  1. settling early inside the window;
  2. that the five candidate measures meet the robustness test, under an unproved assumption that each party’s benefits cover its costs;
  3. that paying in standing and rules rather than power mostly answers objections about reputation;
  4. restraining the language of being first;
  5. pairing openness in a race with stakes that can be split without shifting power;
  6. that warning channels, codes and refusal rights for staff add variety to the follower layer;
  7. the three failure groups, and the rule for combining protections before dominance.

What would change the answer. Within the conditions stated for the mechanism-design results and for the measures, five developments would revise these conclusions:

  • versions of BKM’s model that run over time and resist collusion;
  • measurement of whether misalignment rises or falls with capability;
  • methods of drawing out capability that defeat hiding, monitors of bias that cannot be gamed, or non-catastrophic deterrents in monitor oversight (in place of extreme “trap” actions);
  • reliable ways to draw out a machine’s wants across circumstances and copies;
  • demonstrations that goals which can be fully met, or the restraint devices, can be installed in large pretrained models and survive self-modification and helper machines.

Part 14. What to take away

Inside the window, what can be done about what a machine wants comes down to two things for each lever: where it lives, and how it fails. Filters protect against users. A refusal meant to survive the model’s operators or thieves must live in the trained settings, where retraining can still undo it.

The three existing restraint programs curb action under stated conditions. None changes the machine’s main goal or drives the value of more inputs to zero as measured by that main goal (or net value under attainable utility preservation while the weighted penalty stays below the gain to the main goal; near-definitional), and goals that can be fully met remain an open conjecture. Before dominance, a rising system can be paid in rules, voice, escrowed rewards and standing—never in computing power, freedom to change itself, or control over its own infrastructure—only for wants bounded against what force would win. Once it could take everything, that requires wants that can be fully met, which is unproved.

Above all, the eleven protective factors across the series do not fail independently. Five causes, and the package itself as a caveat, can each defeat several protections or their evidence at once: deception, one training process, a sudden capability jump, release or theft of the weights, and human disunity. My untested judgment is to combine protections across the three failure groups, to reduce shared-cause exposure without escaping it, knowing that human disunity is a cause no mix removes. In that same untested judgment, states and labs should settle early inside the window, with monitoring and renegotiation triggers set in advance while human enforcement holds.

Where to read more

  • Measures That Depend on Ends, the technical paper, gives the formal results with their conditions, the arithmetic, the BKM model, and the actor-by-actor table.
  • The War Baseline supplies the starting assumptions, the range of deals, the promise problem, the forts models, power transition theory and the racing results.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information supplies starting beliefs, the evidence on alignment faking, control setups, pretraining discourse and the AI-risk persuasion tournament and adversarial collaboration, and three of the families of settlement.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict supplies the test for counting a want, the five dimensions of wants, and the three layers of atrocity.
  • Changing the Ends supplies training as the lever on wants, the three conditions for complementarity, the assumption that war needs several conditions at once, and the caveat about the package.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough supplies the two results on whether a machine whose want is met still has a security motive.
  • Many Machines supplies the limits on humanity’s share under a bloc, and the four conditions under which rival machines protect humanity more.
  • Takeoff and Emergence supplies the model of a trailing developer’s lag.
  • Measures That Need No Reading of Ends analyzes the measures that serve here only as the setting.
  • Limits, and an Answer ranks the series’ measures by confidence and applies the robustness test across the series.
  • A Test the Conjecture Could Lose is the series’ pre-registered test of the conjecture about wants.

Full references for the works cited here as “(Name Year)” are in the technical paper.
